name: Yukgunja-tang (East Asian herbal formula; also known as Liujunzi Decoction or Rikkunshito)
short: As rikkunshito, case reports: pneumonitis; meningitis with urinary retention (with another formula); infant low potassium (licorice). Trials: no serious treatment-related events, or none in excess.
text: Names: a 2025 review states that Yukgunja-tang is also known as Liujunzi Decoction or Rikkunshito, a traditional East Asian herbal formula; the cited abstracts do not list its herbs. Case reports under the name rikkunshito (spelled Rikkunshi-to or Rikkunshi-Tou in two reports): a 79-year-old woman was admitted with interstitial pneumonia; all her drugs were stopped and she was given prednisolone, after which she markedly improved, and lymphocyte stimulation and migration inhibition tests were positive for the formula, so the authors diagnosed pneumonitis due to it. A 73-year-old woman taking it together with another formula (Shinbu-Tou) developed subacute meningitis with urinary retention (meningitis-retention syndrome), dermatitis and latent pneumonitis, which the authors attribute likely to the two herbal medicines; all resolved within three weeks of stopping them. An extremely low birth weight infant with gastro-oesophageal reflux disease developed persistent low blood potassium and metabolic alkalosis after treatment with rikkunshito, which resolved gradually after it was stopped and potassium was given; the authors suggest licorice-induced pseudoaldosteronism. Trials under the name yukgunja-tang: in a multicentre, assessor-blind randomized trial in 140 people with functional dyspepsia (56 given yukgunja-tang for 6 weeks), in which safety was a stated outcome, there were no serious treatment-related adverse events in the trial, which also gave a comparator herbal formula to a second group (the abstract does not give the result for each group); milder events are not described. In a pilot randomized trial in 40 people with cancer-related anorexia, comparing the formula plus nutrition counselling with counselling alone, vital signs, ECG, blood and urine tests and adverse events were recorded at every visit, and the numbers and types of adverse events and the laboratory results did not differ between groups. A 2025 meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials (2,086 people) in atrophic gastritis reports fewer adverse events with the formula, alone or added to Western medicine, than with Western medicine alone, with evidence of low or very low certainty. PubMed searches under the names yukgunja-tang and rikkunshito found no report of liver injury, kidney injury or heavy-metal contamination naming the formula. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
